projectDesc.p: The Middle English Texts Series offers a diverse and representative array of literary texts that medieval readers in the present-day British Isles would have encountered between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries. It is committed to making available both affordable print and open access editions to scholars, teachers, and students of the Western Middle Ages. In its digital publications, the series prioritizes a user-friendly interface and viewing options, multiple downloadable formats, enhanced searchability and filtering, and accessibility to the widest possible range of users.

editorialDecl.p: METS takes as its mission the creation of affordable editions that would pass scrutiny from the most demanding expert, yet would prove comprehensible, and even enticing, to someone who had never read Middle English before. This agenda dictates that METS publications offer not a critical edition reflecting all surviving manuscripts, and certainly not a diplomatic edition, but a best-text edition, informed by the notes and apparatus of earlier editions (where these exist), and by substantive variants from other manuscript witnesses. Transcriptions of Middle English texts are lightly modernized to ensure a smooth reading experience, while non-English texts preserve both the original language and a modern English translation in facing-page format. Each edition offers expert assistance with language and lexicon, providing glosses alongside the text(s), textual and explanatory notes, elucidation of unfamiliar contexts and traditions, and thematic and interpretive possibilities. All editions feature general introductions that set the edited text within its own time, place, and traditions, and link it to ancestor, congener, and successor materials. All publications contain comprehensive, current bibliographies of pertinent scholarship and criticism. House style is adapted from the Chicago Manual of Style.

div.p: The Active Policy of a Prince (henceforth: Active Policy) and its addendum Dicta et Opiniones Diversorum Philosophorum (henceforth: Dicta; together: Active Policy and Dicta) were written by George Ashby around the year 1462. The poem is addressed to the Lancastrian crown prince Edward (1453–1471), to whom it is presented as a mirror for princes to prepare him for his future kingship. Ashby, who for most of his professional career worked as clerk in the Lancastrian Signet Office, must have personally known both the crown prince and his parents: as signet clerk, he accompanied the king or queen on their travels throughout the kingdom. As such, Ashby’s work is a vivid testament to the political turbulence of fifteenth-century England. The poem can only be fully understood as a text written at the height of the Wars of the Roses, and specifically by a loyal Lancastrian signet clerk.

The poem comprises two main parts: the first section, entitled Active Policy of a Prince, consists mostly of original Middle English verse with occasional quotations from the Latin wisdom text known as Liber Philosophorum Moralium Antiquorum (The Book of the Ancient Moral Philosophers; henceforth: Liber Philosophorum). The second part, the Dicta et Opiniones Diversorum Philosophorum (The Dicts and Sayings of Diverse Philosophers), is more heavily indebted to the Liber Philosophorum. In this section, Ashby alternates between quotes from his Latin source material and his own Middle English translations of these wise sayings. While the two parts were previously assumed to constitute two different poems, both internal evidence and manuscript evidence show that Ashby conceived of the work as a whole.1

Ashby touches upon a wide range of topics related to contemporary politics and political theory. His advice includes traditional views of good kingship, centered around the cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. In particular, the text continually urges the future king to find wisdom and heed God. In these lessons, the Active Policy and Dicta offers mostly conventional political advice similar to many other mirrors for princes written throughout the medieval period. More particular to the time and place in which Ashby wrote his text was the constant fear of treason and a distrust of both the common people and self-centered counselors. These themes were no doubt influenced by the political realities of Henry VI’s reign, of which Ashby was a close witness.

The poem as a whole does not adhere to a clear structure; it is not divided into sections dealing with specific virtues, such as Thomas Hoccleve’s Regiment for Princes, an important source of inspiration to Ashby. Ashby’s advice is even frequently contradictory: for instance, at various points in the poem he advises the king to always be gracious and merciful, while at the same time he promotes a harsh treatment of anyone who is suspected of treason. These factors complicate questions about the poem’s central message, and even Ashby’s own core political convictions. Concurrently, this tension between competing political views is emblematic of the politically turbulent time in which the poem was written.

Despite the historical relevance of this poem, Ashby’s work is rarely studied — neither the Active Policy and Dicta, nor the Prisoner’s Reflections (or Complaint of a Prisoner in the Fleet), his only other known poem which he wrote as a prisoner in the Fleet prison in 1463.2 Only a handful of publications have discussed Ashby’s poetry to any extent in the last decades, and the Active Policy and Dicta has until now only appeared in print in an 1899 edition by Mary Bateson, which offers no translations of the Latin passages and very few glosses and footnotes. While fifteenth-century English literature — most notably the work of Thomas Hoccleve and John Lydgate — has received increasing attention in recent decades, Ashby is still largely neglected.3 This fact, combined with Sebastian Sobecki’s discovery that the only surviving copy of the Active Policy and Dicta is in fact a holograph, underlines the need for a new edition of this understudied poem.4

The Active Policy and Dicta, in all its manifold political statements and tensions, remains a testimony to the politics of the Wars of the Roses. The full text is here presented in a critical edition with translations of the Latin passages. Preceding the text is a detailed examination of the historical context. After all, the explicit purpose of the Active Policy and Dicta, written at a turbulent moment of English history, is to influence the political reality by equipping the Lancastrian heir with the necessary knowledge and attributes to recover and keep the throne. Understanding the historical background against which the poem was written is therefore essential to grasping the meaning of the text. For this reason, the following introductory material to the edition of the Active Policy and Dicta starts with a discussion of the political developments in the first half of the fifteenth century, culminating in the Wars of the Roses, as well as a description of the development and tasks of the Signet Office, which is indispensable to understanding Ashby’s professional circumstances and his relation to the Crown. The second half of this introduction will focus on the poem itself, its sources, and its only surviving manuscript, as well as the editorial principles employed in the editing of the poem.
Historical context
George Ashby and The Wars of the Roses

George Ashby was born around the year 1385 in the village of Lapworth, Warwickshire. He grew up in an England ruled by Richard II, the last king of the long-lasting Plantagenet dynasty, which had reigned for more than three centuries. Richard’s fall would be the first glimpse that the young George Ashby caught of the instability of political fortune. Richard II was deposed in 1399 by Henry of Lancaster, who assumed the crown as King Henry IV. The suspicious circumstances of Richard’s death during the following year, in addition to the usurpation itself, was a sin that would continue to haunt the Lancastrian dynasty.5 The first Lancastrian king had set a dangerous precedent by deposing a rightful king, one which — successfully or not — others would try to follow in the next century: tellingly, the fear of royal deposition is continually present in the Active Policy and Dicta.

Henry IV was succeeded in 1413 by his son, Henry V. Best remembered for his military achievements in the Hundred Years’ War — most notably the Battle of Agincourt in 1415 — Henry V managed to conquer large swaths of France and consolidated these victories with a diplomatic success when he married Catherine of Valois, the daughter of the French king, Charles VI. In 1420, Henry and Charles agreed upon the Treaty of Troyes, stipulating that the children of Henry and Catherine would be the heirs to both the French and the English thrones — thereby disinheriting the dauphin — and that Henry would act as the regent of France for the remainder of Charles’s life.6 He had good reason to believe that he would eventually be crowned king of France, as Charles was almost twenty years his senior. However, only two years later, Henry died while on campaign to consolidate his position as French regent. His father-in-law survived him by only two months. This meant that Henry and Catherine’s son — and Ashby’s future employer — Henry, an infant of nine months, was proclaimed king of both England and France before his first birthday. By the time Ashby wrote the Active Policy and Dicta over forty years later, the English had lost control over almost all of France — a fact which did not stop Ashby from proclaiming Henry’s son, Prince Edward, the heir to both kingdoms: “Right and myghty prince, and my right goode lorde, / Linially comyn of blode royal, / Bothe of faders and moders of recorde, / Occupying by grace celestial / Thaier roiaulmes” (lines 85–89).

There are no known records of Ashby’s life during these years. We know from later correspondence by Queen Margaret of Anjou that he must have been employed as signet clerk for a younger brother of Henry V, Duke Humphrey of Gloucester, in whose household Ashby probably received his education.7 Ashby would have enjoyed some education before he entered the royal household: young children often received their first training in literacy at home and boys might subsequently be further educated at a grammar school. Through translating Latin poetry, pupils acquired a thorough understanding of grammar, which in turn contributed to the development of vernacular poetry in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.8 The most popular translation exercises were those involving Latin sententiae, short wise sayings or proverbs. An example is the widely used didactic text Distichs of Cato: a form of teaching that Ashby would later incorporate in his political advice, when he presents Latin quotations from the Liber Philosophorum, followed by his Middle English translation in the Dicta (see “Sources for The Active Policy and Dicta,” pp. 20–23, below).

At some point, Ashby entered Gloucester’s household to be further trained as a royal clerk. A royal household was a world of its own, an itinerant structure travelling between great houses, consisting of a family, wards, administrative officials, pages, clerks, and so forth; it was “not just a job, it was a whole way of life.”9 Ashby’s earliest known life record (1426) dates from these years of employment in Gloucester’s household: a nomination by the royal council to receive a pension from the new Bishop of London, probably “at the duke’s prompting,” as Simon Payling suggests.10

From these early years of his professional career, Ashby found himself at the center of the kingdom’s politics. Until the young Henry VI came of age, the kingdom was to be governed by a minority council consisting of the most important peers of the realm, including the Duke of Gloucester.11 In November 1429, when Henry was still only seven years old, he was officially crowned king of England in a lavish display of royal power, and his French coronation followed the next month. In the years after his coronation, Henry increasingly began to take on an active role in government, although the precise extent of his involvement in matters of state remains difficult to determine.12 What did become clear is that Henry would not be the talented statesman that his father was. From the time he was deemed to have reached his majority in 1437 — the year Ashby was transferred from Gloucester’s household to the royal household, to serve as clerk in the newly installed royal Signet Office — Henry began to distribute lands and offices among his favorites, thereby depleting the Crown’s own resources. It is difficult to assess Henry’s personality, let alone his later health problems, from the surviving sources. Most historians agree that Henry was particularly unsuited for the office of kingship, but exactly why, and his degree of involvement in government, remain points of debate.13 Henry may have been a weak-willed king, ruled largely by his council and later by his wife, Queen Margaret. Alternatively, he may at times have assertively enacted his own will, resulting in often undesirable actions, such as the over-generous distribution of lands and other gifts. As a close observer of royal policy from within the household, Ashby would have been aware of the problems of Henry’s reign. Concerns over the protection of unpopular favorites and royal finances are prominent themes of the Active Policy and Dicta. In lines 2011–13, for instance, he cautions against over-generosity: “To graunt over his power, is wastyng / And who that to unnedy wol be graunting / Is not accepted as for man witty.” This engagement with the problems of Henry’s reign is especially prominent at the start of the Active Policy, in the stanzas dealing with the “past time” (lines 127–217). Despite Ashby’s staunch loyalty to the Lancastrian royal family, he does not hesitate to criticize Henry’s policy of harboring favorites who were seen to disrupt the political stability of the realm: “And if [the king] devoided had folke covetous / From his personne, his people had not sterve / With suche grete batellis dispiteous” (lines 191–93).

Whether this criticism is entirely justified remains a point of historical debate, but these lines certainly display the contemporary distrust of powerful royal favorites. One of Henry’s early favorites was William de la Pole, the Earl of Suffolk, who exerted considerable influence over the royal household. Within a few years, he would rise from relatively humble origins — he was not born one of the leading peers of the realm — to become a duke in his own right, despite military failures in the French wars of the 1420s. One of his most significant actions during the 1440s was his involvement in the marriage negotiations between Henry VI and the French noblewoman Margaret of Anjou. The young couple were married in 1445, under a treaty securing a two-year truce between the French and the English. George Ashby was among the delegation who accompanied Margaret from France to England, and it is presumably around this moment that Ashby was appointed as the queen’s personal signet clerk. Margaret brought with her the promise of peace: upon her arrival in England, she was hailed as the peace bringer during her procession through London.14 However, as the daughter of Count René of Anjou, King of Naples and Jerusalem in name only, she brought no new lands or riches with her. To the contrary, as part of the marriage settlement Suffolk had promised to return Maine and Anjou to the French, thus exposing Normandy to a French invasion. After the English alliance with the Duchy of Brittany failed, Normandy was quickly conquered by the French. In 1450, Normandy was lost, and Gascony followed soon after. Within a few years, the English lands in France were reduced to only the port town of Calais.

It was Suffolk who bore the blame for these failures, and who was subsequently charged with treason by the commons in 1449. Despite Henry’s attempts to protect Suffolk, the latter was eventually brought to justice and, with Henry’s intervention, punished by a banishment of five years. It looked as if Suffolk had survived relatively unscathed, but during his sea voyage to France he was captured and beheaded “in the name of the ‘community of the realm.’”15 He was not the only victim of public unrest in the year 1450. That same year, a great uprising started in Kent under the leadership of a man called Jack Cade. The grievances arose from the loss of the lands in France, the concomitant decrease of trade, and economic recession. Though presenting themselves as “the commons of England,” the rebels were people from all layers of the English population, including the gentry, who claimed they felt compelled to stand up for the common good.16 Their complaints were largely aimed at Suffolk and his associates, whom they saw as corrupting good government.17 They did not seek any constitutional change, but said they wanted to liberate the king from his counselors’ harmful influence, and in their place restore the “natural” counselor of the king: the most powerful peer of the realm, Richard, Duke of York. At this time, York was a lieutenant in Ireland, and arguably had no hand in the rising. Yet after being proclaimed the savior of the commons, York returned to England in September, just two months after Jack Cade’s Rebellion had ravaged the city of London. Cade himself had by then already been arrested and executed. For the time being the rebellion was over, but the grievances remained. York now saw himself cast into the role of spokesperson for the common people, in opposition to what was seen to be a corrupt government dominated by unpopular royal favorites.

York not only enjoyed popular support, he was also the first in line to inherit the throne if Henry and Margaret should fail to produce an heir. However, he was not the only one eager to fill the power vacuum left behind after Suffolk’s demise. Another peer of the realm, Edmund Beaufort, Duke of Somerset, also returned to England and soon gained Henry’s trust to become the new royal favorite. In response, York gravitated towards a position of opposition to the royal government. One of his main points of criticism concerned the royal finances: following Suffolk’s patronage policy, Somerset continued to grant lands and offices to bind people to the regime, while York advocated for a resumption of all of these grants to remedy the Crown’s increasing financial problems.18 Interestingly, Ashby likewise frequently cautions the prince to guard his spending and tightly control the Crown’s revenues: “Caste you to live of youre own properté, / Of youre revenues, lyvelode, and rent, / Propornoning after the quantité / Youre expenses by youre owne jugement” (lines 274–77). Still, most lords of the realm continued to support the king, and hence the rule from his household, instead of the opposition led by York. The Duke of York seemed barred from playing any meaningful role in central government, and his attempts to carve out a role for himself failed, despite popular support.19

This could have spelled the end of York’s political career, were it not for the illness that befell Henry VI in August 1453. The king had fallen into a catatonic state: not even the birth of his first son, Edward, in October 1453 could elicit any response from Henry. The King’s Council tried to keep his condition secret, but it was clear that something needed to be done to keep the government afloat. York, as the most powerful peer of the realm, was invited back to the Council. Despite a bid for power from Queen Margaret, York was given the title of Lord Protector on March 27, 1454, which meant that he effectively governed the kingdom. However, soon after the king recovered in February 1455, York was stripped of his protectorate and many of his decisions were reversed. York and his allies, the Nevilles, retreated to the north and, fearing that they would be destroyed by the Great Council that the king had summoned in Leicester, gathered their troops to march south. Somerset and the king did not have time to raise an army, and likely did not expect to need one. But York’s tactics this time were very different from before. He did not appeal for widespread but unreliable popular support; instead, he quickly marched south. Nor did he wait for an audience with the king to press his demands, but he attacked the king’s army at St Albans. This was the greatest departure from normal political practice so far, and it laid the groundwork for the increasingly forceful acts of rebellion that were to follow in the next decade20 — a reality that pervades Ashby’s political thinking. He frequently expresses fears of treason and rebellion in the Active Policy and Dicta. His advice in lines 1653–54 to never make any person equal to the king in power and means (“Yeve never power, ne auctorité / To no maner persoune on erthe lyvyng”) is followed by the arresting image that such a person will otherwise “set his fote uppon your nekke” (line 1658). Although York and Neville later claimed that they had not seen the king’s banner raised, everyone knew that what they had done was nothing less than treason. During the skirmish — it could hardly be called a battle — in St Albans, Somerset (the royal favorite) and two other lords were killed. York had thus managed to remove his greatest enemy, but at the price of shedding first blood in what had now become a civil war.

During the battle, York had also managed to capture Henry, thus securing his hold on government. With the power now once more in the hands of the Yorkists, they were quick to show that their loyalty was still with the king. Emphasizing that they had not committed treason, but were forced to do what they had done by the actions of Somerset and his allies, the rebel lords presented themselves as loyal subjects of the crown. With the backing of the commons, York was again made Lord Protector on November 12, 1455. Ironically, the need for York’s protectorate to restore the peace was partly caused by his own game-changing actions in St Albans, which seem to have paved the way for any nobleman with a grievance to resort to violence.21 Ashby, now working as signet clerk for Queen Margaret, saw these events unfold from up close: it is therefore no surprise that the constant threat of dissension and rebellion is a prominent theme in the Active Policy and Dicta.

Even if York was for now Lord Protector, this did not mean he had full power over the kingdom — or, indeed, even over the king. However popular York and his demands for reform may have been with the commons, it was clear that the lords were not ready to supplant an anointed king. Although York continued to pursue his policy of resumption of earlier grants, his measures were not yet fully implemented before Henry was requested by the lords to resume control in February 1456. With Suffolk and Somerset gone, it was now Queen Margaret who assumed the greatest influence over the king. Having provided the kingdom with an heir, she felt secure enough in her position to begin to assert political influence, although her actions were always framed within the bounds of acceptable behavior for a medieval queen.22 Despite Ashby’s close proximity to the queen in these years, the Active Policy and Dicta contains remarkably few references to women or queenship, perhaps precisely because this was such a controversial topic.

As relations continued to deteriorate, Henry, as ever in favor of peace, made York and Margaret bury their differences on Loveday in 1458. In a grand procession through London on what was then the first day of the new year (March 25), the Yorkist and Lancastrian supporters made open displays of reconciliation. Yet the underlying causes for the distrust between the queen and the duke had not been resolved, nor had the victims of the Yorkist aggression at St Albans been forgotten. The Yorkists continued to openly defy royal authority, while distributing letters in which they emphasized that they were acting as the king’s loyal subjects to protect the common good.23 When the situation became untenable and a military confrontation seemed inevitable, many Yorkist supporters refused to openly commit treason. Their faction fell apart, and York and his closest associates fled abroad.

That same year, the Coventry Parliament, later known as Parliament of Devils, in which George Ashby served as MP for Warwickshire, passed an attainder of the Yorkist lords.24 This meant that they were stripped of their lands and inheritance, the harshest punishment possible for the nobility that based their power on land. It may have reminded the elderly Ashby of what had happened to Henry VI’s grandfather, Henry Bolingbroke, who was stripped of his inheritance by Richard II in 1398 and who returned a year later to usurp the English throne. Judging from his advice on how to deal with traitors in the Active Policy and Dicta, though, Ashby seems to have been in favor of forceful measures against traitors: he urges the Lancastrian prince “to suppresse your false conspiratours / Aftur the lawe and constitucion / Establisshed ayenst opyn traitorous” (lines 381–83) and to “subdewe with al suppressyng / Every personne withoute submission / Pretendyng right to youre coronacion” (lines 417–19). However, like the Lancastrian duke more than sixty years before, York would not sit by idly while all his possessions were taken from him. From a safe distance in Ireland, he started to gather support for his return to England, while his allies Warwick and Salisbury, who had also been attainted, did the same in Calais. The Yorkists and their armies returned to England in June 1460 and managed to defeat the Lancastrian army. Though they captured Henry, the Yorkists continued to profess loyalty to the king, and claimed that they had been acting for the country’s good. Henry was still king in name, but it was clear that he was now ruled by the Yorkists’ wishes: in October 1460, Parliament convened to revoke the attainder of the Yorkists.

So far, the situation seemed similar to the aftermath of the First Battle of St Albans, but this time the Duke of York’s own plans were very different. Despite his allies’ professed loyalty to Henry VI, York, upon his return, did not hesitate to claim the crown for himself. When he arrived in London on October 13, he laid his hands on the throne.25 It is unclear whether this was according to a previous agreement between York and his allies, or whether it was his own decision. It was the first time York openly expressed his wish to take the crown for himself, instead of professing to be Henry’s loyal servant.26 Until then, the struggle had explicitly been about governance and the common good, as well as York’s right to counsel the king as the most powerful magnate of the realm; from now on, it developed into a dynastic dispute.

However, York had overplayed his hand, and the lords refused to assent to the removal of a king who was not seen as a tyrant — as had been the case with Richard II — but merely as a weak king. York continued to press his case, and convinced Parliament to approve the agreement known as the Act of Accord, which ruled that Henry VI would remain king but that his son Prince Edward, in whose education Ashby was probably involved around this time, would be supplanted as heir to the throne by York.27 Queen Margaret and Prince Edward, who not only lost his position as heir but also all his revenues, would of course not assent to this, and they made preparations to meet the Yorkists on the battlefield. At the Battle of Wakefield on December 30, the Lancastrian army won a decisive victory.28 It was a devastating blow for the Yorkist cause: Duke Richard of York was killed. As a mockery of York’s royal aspirations, his decapitated head was displayed publicly with a paper crown. It is likely that George Ashby, as signet clerk to the queen, accompanied the Lancastrian army on their campaign, and these events may have influenced his views on how the king should deal with rebel lords.

Despite this Lancastrian victory, according to the terms of the Act of Accord, York’s son Edward was still the heir presumptive. With the Lancastrian royal family (including the now liberated king) still in the north, there could be no more pretense that the new Duke of York ruled as regent on behalf of Henry VI. He now judged the time ripe to finalize his father’s ambitions. Claiming that he was no longer bound to the terms of the Act of Accord because Henry had broken it by fleeing, Edward claimed the crown for himself. With two crowned kings in one kingdom, all peers of the realm were now forced to choose sides. Edward consolidated his claim by winning a decisive victory at the Battle of Towton. The Lancastrian royal family was forced to flee to Scotland, while Edward IV returned victoriously to London.

Based on both internal and archival evidence, it seems most likely that Ashby wrote the Active Policy and Dicta around this time (see “Date of composition,” p. 15, below). It is telling that he never explicitly acknowledges the fact that a Yorkist king was then occupying the throne, or even that there was a rival claim to the throne at all, even though he does refer to Henry’s and Margeret’s reign in the past tense (“Ever thaught grete was their mayestee,” line 96). Some Lancastrian retainers, such as Sir John Fortescue, joined the royal family in exile. Ashby did not; to the contrary, he was imprisoned in the Fleet in 1462, possibly on account of his Lancastrian sympathies,29 like many others who remained loyal to Henry and Margaret. While imprisoned, he wrote his only other known poem: the Prisoner’s Reflections, written between Michaelmas 1463 and March 24, 1464.30 In this poem, Ashby recounts how he is imprisoned “[b]y a gret commaundment of a lord / To whom I must obey for hys gret myght, / Though I cannat therto sadly acord [seriously agree].”31 Later, he expands on this by claiming that “[b]ecause of my draught and my bryngyng up, / I have suffryd thys and other spoylyng,” suggesting that his current plight is caused by his Lancastrian background.32 Possibly it was his involvement in the Parliament of Devils that was the direct reason for Yorkist retaliation, though if this is the case, Ashby’s imprisonment came rather late after the Yorkist victory. Sobecki reconstructs the most likely starting date of Ashby’s incarceration as between late summer and September 28, 1462.33 Another potential explanation for his imprisonment advanced by Sobecki is the composition of the Active Policy and Dicta, which formed undeniable proof of his Lancastrian sympathies. It is unknown how much longer after the composition of the prison poem Ashby remained in the Fleet. He must have been released some time before March 22, 1465, which is the first time he reappears in the records.34

While Ashby thus remained behind in England, Margaret and her son attempted to reignite the Lancastrian cause from a rival court set up in France, consisting of between fifty and two hundred Lancastrian courtiers.35 It was a small and impoverished court, though the presence of the lawyer-propagandist Sir John Fortescue, who also wrote a political advice text for Prince Edward, known as In Praise of the Laws of England, “gave the court a cultural identity, albeit a rather sombre one.”36 Margaret was relentless in her search for allies who might help the Lancastrians regain the English throne, which she eventually found in an unlikely alliance with the former Yorkist supporter, the Earl of Warwick. After a ceremonial apology by Warwick and a reconciliation with the Lancastrian exiles, they signed the Treaty of Angers in 1470 which reinstated Henry VI as king, though the country would be ruled by his son Prince Edward and a council.

Perhaps it now seemed to Ashby that his Active Policy and Dicta might fulfill its purpose in advising the Lancastrian Prince Edward on how to be a good king after all. Ashby must have watched the events unfold over the following months with great excitement. He had witnessed two successful invasions from France — Henry Bolingbroke’s in 1399 and the Yorkists’ in 1460–1461. This time, however, there was no success: despite initial military victories, the Lancastrians were eventually defeated by the Yorkist troops at the Battle of Tewkesbury, and Prince Edward of Lancaster was among the casualties of the battle. A few weeks later, Henry VI died under suspicious circumstances, too, undoubtedly at the command of Edward IV. York’s victory was now far more complete than it had been in 1461. It seemed the Lancastrian cause was finally extinguished. Margaret was imprisoned in England until 1475, after which she returned to France to live out her days with her family.

George Ashby retired from public life, and died at his Breakspear estate in Middlesex in 1474. The royal family he had served his whole life was defeated, and the young prince he had counselled on how to be a good king had been killed at the age of seventeen before having had a chance to put Ashby’s political advice into practice. It must have been a hard blow for the octogenarian poet, who had spent more than a year in prison, presumably on account of his Lancastrian sympathies. Though neither he nor his contemporaries could know it, however, the Wars of the Roses were not over: the Yorkists were to be overthrown by Henry Tudor in 1485, who traced his claim to the throne via his mother, Margaret Beaufort, a descendant of John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster. Ashby did not live to see this return of the Lancastrian bloodline to the throne. His son and grandson, however, followed in their father’s footsteps to serve as signet clerks: his grandson and namesake, George, would serve under Henry VII and Henry VIII, the Tudor monarchs who based their legitimacy on their Lancastrian descent.37
The Signet Office

At the start of the Active Policy, in the Latin proem preceding the Middle English verse, Ashby identifies himself as a clerk of the Signet Office. As such, he inscribes not only his own identity but also his professional occupation explicitly into his text. It is his position at the center of government, and in the vicinity of the Lancastrian royal family, on which he bases his authority as a wise advisor on political matters. Political advice was not usually the task of signet clerks, as their professional duties were limited to administrative matters. Informally, however, it seems likely that signet clerks like Ashby, who were members of the frequently itinerant royal household and who were responsible for the king’s and queen’s personal correspondence, wielded some limited influence. There is in fact evidence that signet clerks and in particular the Secretary, the head of the Signet Office, were viewed with some suspicion by critics of the royal government since the office’s inception in the fourteenth century, on account of their close proximity to the royal family.

Seals played an important role in medieval correspondence and governance. They were used not only by the Crown, but also by noblemen and other important individuals and institutions. Seals usually held an image of a person or their coat of arms, and were pressed into beeswax to close a letter. In this way, they were proof of a document’s authenticity: in other words, to show that the letter really was issued by the person or institution who held the seal. By the late fourteenth century, there were three governmental writing offices in function, each of which used a different seal: Chancery held the great seal, for the most official documents; the Privy Seal Office held the privy seal, for less formal documents; and the Signet Office held the signet or secret seal, for the king’s personal correspondence.38 The oldest and largest of the three late medieval writing offices, originating in its basic form in the pre-Conquest period, was Chancery. Documents issued by Chancery were official and authoritative, ordered by the king or in some cases by members of the Council, and authenticated by the great seal. Such documents included, for instance, grants of titles or lands, summons to Parliament, and official orders and pardons. The great seal was kept by the Chancellor, the highest official of Chancery, and hundreds of clerks generated the output, ranging from senior clerks responsible for the rolls to junior clerks who wrote simple writs.

Centuries earlier, Chancery had already become too large to travel with the king and had become fixed in Westminster. A second writing office, the Privy Seal Office, was in use from around the early thirteenth century to manage royal correspondence when the king was not in Westminster. This office, headed by the Keeper of the privy seal, was responsible for issuing warrants to Chancery which ordered the issue of official letters under the great seal, in addition to many other types of letters. Evidence of the wide array of activities of the Privy Seal Office can be found in the formulary compiled by Thomas Hoccleve, a clerk of the privy seal, with whose poetical works George Ashby was certainly familiar.39 While the Privy Seal Office was originally the private writing office of the king, in time, it also grew too large to travel with the king and became fixed in Westminster.

A third, smaller writing office was therefore established in the fourteenth century: the Signet Office, consisting of the Secretary, who was the Keeper of the seal, a handful of clerks, and some servants. It probably grew from the king’s “secret” seal, which came to be called the signet.40 Many of the records about the origins and development of the office are lost, since the signet records were destroyed in a fire in the seventeenth century.41 While the Signet Office presumably filed draft letters like the Privy Seal Office and Chancery,42 the loss of these documents means that the office’s history and activities can now only be gained from signet letters kept in other archives, such as Chancery’s records or local archives. Drawing extensively on these surviving sources, J. Otway-Ruthven traces the origins of the signet seal to the reign of Edward II, though it is only under Richard II’s rule that the Signet Office appears as an organized department.43

Contrary to the other writing offices, the Signet Office remained itinerant as part of the royal household. Though in principle stationed at Windsor Castle, the clerks and Secretary were expected to accompany the king or his consort on their travels to take care of their correspondence, a function that was especially important during Henry V’s campaigns in France. The role of the Secretary (MED: “one entrusted with private or confidential matters”, “a trusted servant or counselor”)44 was foremost that of a confidant in charge of the king’s secrets — a responsibility that would be constantly at the forefront of Ashby’s mind while he wrote the Active Policy and Dicta (“Kepe secretnesse as a secretarye,” he notes in line 354; on the office of the Secretary, he advises the prince to find “a Secretarie withe inspeccion, / Secrete, sad, and of goode intencion,” lines 467–68). At this time, the Secretary was a courtier rather than a public administrative official. It is only in the sixteenth century that the Secretary became one of the most influential ministers. The Signet Office similarly lacked the authority and official role enjoyed by Chancery and, to a lesser extent, the Privy Seal Office. The signet seal was mainly used for the king’s own correspondence and to send “letters missive,” that is, letters from the king containing commands to officials.45 It was not uncommon for the Signet Office to send a letter to the Privy Seal Office requesting that a letter authenticated by the privy seal be sent to Chancery, in order for an official warrant authenticated with the great seal to be issued.46 In practice, the division of tasks between the Signet Office and the Privy Seal Office was not very strict. It seems often to have been a matter of convenience, where the latter mostly represented orders issued from the authority of the council, and the former represented those of the king.47

The Secretary and the clerks, like Ashby, would have accompanied their royal employers in their travels both in England and abroad. A concise description of the duties of the signet clerks is found in Ashby’s own words, at the start of A Prisoner’s Reflections, in which he describes his occupation as follows:

lg.l: Wrytyng to theyre sygnet full fourty yere
As well beyond the see as on thys syde,
Doyng my servyce as well there as here,
Nat sparyng for to go ne for to ryde,
Havyng pen and inke evyr at my syde,
As truly as I coude to theyre entent
Redy to acomplysshe theyre commandment.48

div.p: While Secretaries might be promoted to higher functions, signet clerks usually remained in office for their lifetime, political circumstances permitting. The main activities of Ashby and his colleagues consisted of the writing of letters, though they might also be employed in various other duties, including assistance on diplomatic missions. Remaining sources suggest that the total yearly output of the three writing offices amounted to some 30,000 to 40,000 records, around half of which were issued under the privy and signet seal.49 A clerk like Ashby, then, might have been responsible for writing around 500 letters missive per year, as well as other types of documents.50

When the Signet Office first appeared in the records in the later years of Richard II’s reign, its function was comparatively limited, being more involved in the king’s private matters rather than affairs of state. The Parliament records of Richard II’s deposition show that, as the king’s most personal writing office, the signet was seen to express the king’s own will more directly than the other offices.51 Its use was greatly expanded by Richard II in the 1380s, to the point that it almost replaced the Privy Seal Office. This development was met with suspicion by officials of government and the King’s Council. After all, the Council had no influence over nor clear sight of the activities of the Signet Office; while the Chancellor and the Keeper of the privy seal were both members of the Council, the Secretary was not.

Though almost the entire signet staff was replaced at the accession of Henry IV,52 the writing office continued to be in use under the Lancastrian kings. When Henry V died, however, and Henry VI became king at a mere nine months old, the impact on the king’s personal writing office was vast. Even though a Secretary seems to have been appointed after Henry’s coronation in 1429, he was dismissed in 1432. Between 1432 and 1437, in the absence of a Secretary, the king’s signet was kept in the Exchequer and “sealed up under the signet of the Duke of Gloucester.”53 Gloucester’s influence over the king and his household is apparent from the fact that Henry’s first Secretary was Thomas Beckington, who had been Gloucester’s Chancellor.54 George Ashby, who had been a signet clerk in Gloucester’s household for some years, was at this time also transferred to the King’s Signet Office.55 Shortly after Henry’s marriage to Margaret of Anjou, Ashby was appointed signet clerk to the queen (senior members of the royal household often had their own secretarial staff).56

A mark of the close connection between the signet and the king’s individual will is the fact that upon his accession in 1399, Henry IV revoked only grants authenticated with the signet seal, and not any of those issued under the great seal.57 Otway-Ruthven concludes that “the record [of this revocation] seems in fact to be the expression of a distinction between the public and private capacities of the king.”58 In other words, whereas documents issued under the great seal were apparently seen to represent the public duties of the Crown, the signet seal was regarded as expressing an individual king’s private will. This distinction is especially pertinent in the case of Henry VI. One of the complaints often filed against him, both by contemporaries and later historians, is that his private will seemed to be lacking, and that he did not have the force of will to make his own independent decisions. Yet the Council seems to have continued to regard the Signet Office with suspicion, particularly in cases when the signet seal was used to directly procure a document from Chancery, instead of through the intermediary Privy Seal Office which was supervised by a Council member.59 Indeed, the influence of the signet staff — the Secretary as well as clerks — might have been even more suspicious because of Henry’s perceived weakness. The Secretary, for instance, was responsible for summonses to the king, and therefore had considerable influence over who had access to him.

The clerks, too, seem to have had some influence over “legal business and minor appointments.”60 Ashby and his fellow clerks would have had very close access to the inner workings of politics, being always at the king’s or the queen’s side. As such, signet clerks were more than not administrative officials; as John Scattergood explains, “[t]hey were accustomed to receiving orders and instruction and, because they had some authority and responsibility for others, accustomed to giving orders and instruction too [. . .] they listened and were listened to, they learned and they taught.”61 Concerns about the influence exercised over the king is often central to the complaints filed against government in the fifteenth century, both from the commons and from peers. As Otway-Ruthven concludes, “the suspicion with which they [the Secretary and signet clerks] were not infrequently regarded shows that under a weak king they were thought to have opportunities to exercise a considerable influence.”62

Though Ashby was only a clerk, and in this capacity had no direct influence on government, the treatment of the staff members of the Signet Office during political crises emphasizes that they were seen to be more political than their colleagues at the other writing offices. Virtually the entire staff of the office was replaced after the various dynastic transitions of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries: in 1399, in 1461, and again in 1485.63 Moreover, Secretaries and even signet clerks, such as Ashby’s contemporaries John Blakeney and William Joseph, were sometimes accused of abusing their political influence.64 The former was included in a list of people whom the commons demanded be dismissed from the king’s service in 1451, because they were accused of having a corrupting influence on the king.65 The latter, William Joseph, clerk of the king’s signet, was one of the three men accused by the Yorkists of withholding crucial information from Henry VI in the approach to the First Battle of St Albans in 1455; the other two men were the Duke of Somerset and the Speaker of the House, Thomas Thorpe.66 While Somerset was the prime rival of the Duke of York at this time, and Speaker Thorpe had presented condemning articles against York, the accusation of a mere clerk like Joseph is more difficult to explain. C. A. J. Armstrong suggests that “perhaps his inclusion was intended to emphasize the baseness of the clique which was supposed to have controlled the king.”67

These instances show the extent to which signet clerks could be, and were perceived to be, political men. Professionally tied to the king’s household, whether itinerant or in Windsor, many of these clerks must have become personally involved with the welfare of the royal family. That seems, at the very least, to have been the case for George Ashby, whose loyalty to his Lancastrian employers prompted him to write a highly partisan text under exceptionally sensitive political circumstances, for a young prince whom he might have regarded as his pupil. The political views expressed in the Active Policy and Dicta were undoubtedly influenced by Ashby’s position as a signet clerk, whose whole profession revolved around the personal will of the king and queen.
Date of composition

The precise date of composition of the Active Policy and Dicta is crucial to understanding the meaning and goal of a text written in such a politically turbulent time. There is no conclusive evidence for the exact time of writing, and various suggestions have been put forward. Theoretically, the poem could have been written at any time during Edward of Lancaster’s lifetime (1453–1471). On the basis of both internal and external evidence, however, a dating of 1461–1462 seems most likely.

In lines 96 and 97, Ashby refers to the reign of Henry IV and Queen Margaret in the past tense: “grete was their mayestee” and “they eschewed vengeance and rigoure.” Moreover, in the Latin proem Ashby refers to himself as “nuper clericum Signeti suppreme domine nostre Margarete” (lately clerk of the signet for our supreme lady Margaret). This suggests that the poem was written after Henry VI was deposed by Edward IV in March 1461.68 Roughly a year and a half after the Yorkist usurpation, around late summer 1462, Ashby was imprisoned in the Fleet Prison.69 Under these political circumstances, it seems unlikely that Ashby wrote his staunchly Lancastrian political poem while he remained in prison, not to mention that he must have had access to his source material while composing the text. It is unknown when Ashby was released from prison: he makes his first appearance in the surviving life records in 1465. Previous critics have suggested Ashby then joined the Lancastrian court in exile and wrote the Active Policy and Dicta from there, as part of the Lancastrian campaign to prepare for their return to England.70 However, new archival evidence suggests that Ashby stayed in England after his release from prison and that he retired from public life.71 Rather than engaging with the political situation by writing an advice poem for a prince in exile, Ashby, who by then was eighty years old, seems to have been concerned with securing his lands and possessions for his family. A later composition date therefore seems unlikely.

The manuscript evidence further strengthens this proposed date of composition.72 The only surviving manuscript of the Active Policy and Dicta, Cambridge University Library, MS Mm.4.42, is a holograph. The manuscript is unfinished; illuminated capitals, for which space was left on the manuscript pages, were never added. If the text was part of a concerted effort to bolster the Lancastrian claim that started in 1468, the manuscript would have had to be finished before the Lancastrian invasion of England in 1471. It is difficult to account for the unfinished state of the manuscript if it was written at the Lancastrian court in France as part of their propaganda prior to the invasion.73 Until and unless new evidence comes to light, the most likely window of opportunity for Ashby to have composed the Active Policy and Dicta is therefore from April 1461 to the second half of 1462: following the defeat of the Lancastrian royal family, but before his imprisonment and retirement from political life.
The text
Form and structure

The main text of Ashby’s poem is preceded by a Latin prose preface in which Ashby identifies himself and his dedicatee, and explains the purpose of his text. He presents himself as a loyal signet clerk of “our supreme lady Margaret, Queen of England,” and professes his loyalty to “his mightiest and most excellent lord, Edward,” Margaret’s son and the Lancastrian prince to whom Ashby’s poem is dedicated. Ashby here also announces the structure of the poem, and explains how it is to be read by its addressee. The prince, as Ashby suggests, is perfectly capable of distilling wise lessons from the material presented here.

The Middle English poem is divided into a collection of increasingly lengthy sections. After twelve introductory stanzas, the subtitle “De activa pollecia principis” (on the active policy of the prince) marks the start of the political advice. As announced in the prose preface, this section of the poem is divided into three parts, touching upon the past, the present, and the future. Following this tripartite section of mostly original Middle English text, the bulk of the poem, under the heading “Dicta et opiniones diversorum philosophorum” (the dicts and sayings of diverse philosophers), presents Latin quotations from the Liber Philosophorum Moralium Antiquorum, a collection of Latin wisdom that was highly popular in late medieval Europe.74 This half of the poem is no longer divided into coherent sections dealing with the past, present, and the future. In fact, it is difficult to discern a coherent structure in this section of the poem at all. The prose quotations are of unequal length, all followed by one or very occasionally two seven-line rhyme royal stanzas with Ashby’s Middle English translations, covering a wide range of themes. Unlike, for instance, in Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes, here there is no clear division into coherent sections dealing with thematically related lessons on kingship.

The division of the poem into two parts — the Active Policy and the Dicta — has led some to view the advice text as two separate poems, but the identification of CUL MS Mm.4.42 as a holograph shows that Ashby clearly intended the texts to be read as a whole, consisting of two separate but related sections.75 The interconnectedness of the texts is also apparent from the use of the Latin sayings of the philosophers in both parts of the poem. While the Dicta makes most use of these maxims, the Latin quotations occasionally appear in the Active Policy. For that reason, to refer to the work as a whole, it is most accurate to use the full title: the Active Policy of a Prince & Dicta et Opiniones Diversorum Philosophorum, or Active Policy and Dicta in short.

The poem ends in the middle of the 312th stanza. Because there are no other textual witnesses, it is impossible to determine how much of the text is missing. There is no indication in the text that Ashby was working towards a conclusion. Neither can we determine it on the basis of his source material, since Ashby was not translating the Liber Philosophorum systematically from beginning to end, but rather seemed to have chosen passages that were relevant to the point he wished to make.
Language and versification

Ashby’s Middle English is fairly understandable to the modern reader, representing the southern variant that is the precursor to modern English. Ashby’s proficiency in both Latin and French is evident in his vocabulary: his verse is marked by frequent use of words deriving from French. Moreover, the Active Policy and Dicta is a macaronic text: in addition to the Middle English verse, there are many passages in Latin which Ashby took from his source material. There are occasional grammatical lapses in these Latin passages, which could either be due to copying mistakes on Ashby’s part or mistakes in his exemplar, which is as yet unidentified. Where relevant, this edition provides variant readings from other manuscripts of the Liber Philosophorum (see “Editorial principles,” pp. 25–27, below).

In both the Active Policy and Dicta and his only other known poem, the Prisoner’s Reflections, Ashby employs the rhyme royal form, characterized by the ABABBCC rhyme scheme, first introduced to English poetry by Geoffrey Chaucer. Moreover, like much of Chaucer’s verse, the Active Policy and Dicta is written in decasyllabic lines, though there are occasional irregularities. Final -e’s are usually silent in the Active Policy and Dicta. The usual rhythmic pattern of the verse lines is iambic pentameter, with alternating stressed (in boldface font) and unstressed syllables:

lg.l: Alas, saufe Goddes wille and his plesaunce,
That ever ye shulde dye and chaunge this lyffe,
Untyl tyme that, by youre wise pourveunce
Ye had lafte to us sum remembratife
Of a personne, lerned and inventif,
Disposed aftur youre condicion
Of fresshe makyng, to oure instruction.
(lines 8–14)

div.p: The metrical pattern shows that final -e is usually silent in Ashby’s verse, while -ion (as in “condicion,” line 13 above) consists of two syllables. Though the metrical pattern of the stanza quoted just now is fairly regular, this is indeed not always the case. Ashby often reverses the stress pattern of feet, as in line 12 (of a personne, lerned . . .), where he substitutes iambs (unstressed-stressed) with trochees (stressed-unstressed). While his lines are usually decasyllabic, they are not always easy to scan smoothly.

Ashby himself clearly viewed his poetry in the tradition of the greatest Middle English verse. The opening lines of the Active Policy invoke his “maisters Gower, Chaucer, and Lydgate,” the “Primier poetes of this nacion, / Embelysshing oure Englisshe tendure algate.” His later professions that his poetry is inadequate, and he a mere “blondryng [. . .] pentise” (lines 26, 28) following Chaucer’s great example, should be read more as deference to the ubiquitous humility topos in late medieval verse than as a true confession of his supposed poetic incompetence.76 At the same time, it is unfair to judge Ashby’s poetry from the standards set by Chaucer, Gower, and even Lydgate. There is no evidence that Ashby had literary ambitions before he felt compelled by political events to start writing a versified mirror for princes, which was after all the accepted form for social inferiors to present advice to royalty. To get his political message across, Ashby’s verse is perfectly adequate, despite occasional irregularities in meter and rhyme.
Genre: Mirrors for princes and the tradition of political advice

Much ink has been spilled to describe the development of the mirrors for princes tradition from antiquity well into the early modern age. While most mirrors date from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, advice for kings on how to govern has existed as long as there have been kings. Throughout the early Middle Ages, advice texts for kings were mostly geared towards the moral aspect of good kingship by focusing on his personal attributes.77 As God’s vicar on earth, it was the king’s task to lead his people to salvation through his personal virtue by imitating Christ.78 The emphasis in these manuals was on obedience to God, religious and moral virtues, and the proper conduct of the king’s own person, as well as his duty to the people. Usually seen as the starting point of the development of the mirrors for princes in the High Middle Ages is John of Salisbury’s influential Policraticus (ca. 1159).79 Although this work touches on many aspects of society, ethics, and court life, the discussions about the body politic and the relation between king and people are the most famous and influential parts of Policraticus. According to John of Salisbury’s definition of kingship, a king necessarily has his people’s best interest at heart: if he does not protect the common good but only pursues his own personal goals, he is a tyrant rather than a lawful king and may thus rightfully be deposed.80 Policraticus remained one of the most influential medieval political texts. In particular its passages on tyranny and the body politic — concepts that would be highly relevant in Lancastrian England — were often used in later political writings throughout the medieval West. Following the rediscovery of Aristotle’s Politics and Nicomachean Ethics, the emphasis of mirrors for princes began to shift from a narrow focus on moral aspects of kingship to an increased attention to the political duties of a king. Influenced by classical political philosophy, the image of the king veered away from God’s shepherd on earth to the embodiment of the political kingdom.81 In addition to the traditional moral virtues recommended to the king, more emphasis began to be placed on his administrative and legislative duties.

Giles of Rome’s highly influential De Regimine Principum (On the Governance of Princes; ca. 1278) is usually credited with making Aristotle’s political thoughts successfully relevant for the medieval Christian world.82 However, another (pseudo-)Aristotelian tradition, though far less studied today, was equally popular in the Middle Ages: the lengthy classical collections of wise sayings transmitted to Western Europe via Arabic sources. Though Western and Eastern mirrors for princes are often studied in isolation from each other, the traditions have much in common and certainly influenced each other.83 The most direct influence from Islamic sources in the medieval West occurred through these compilations of pseudo-Aristotelian teachings. Among these was the Arabic text Mokhtâr el-Hikam (The Choicest Maxims and Best Sayings; Latin title: Liber Philosophorum Moralium Antiquorum; The Book of the Ancient Moral Philosophers), Ashby’s primary source (see “Sources for The Active Policy and Dicta,” pp. 20–23, below). An even more popular collection of maxims was the Secretum Secretorum (The Secret of Secrets), from the originally Arabic source Kitāb sirr al-asrār (The Secret of Secrets), the earliest fragments of which survive from the tenth century.84 The texts certainly seemed to reach their royal target audience: Steven J. Williams has shown that the Secretum Secretorum was a popular addition to royal libraries in Western Europe, though it remains doubtful whether many kings actually read the lengthy work.85

These two related traditions, the mirrors and the maxims, come together in the two parts of Ashby’s advice poem, in the Active Policy and Dicta, respectively. In addition to these two types of wisdom literature, a third related tradition of political instruction was equally popular in the Middle Ages: that of the de casibus. These are collections of exempla, narratives from biblical or classical history, that, according to traditional definitions, serve to illustrate certain moral or political lessons. Despite or perhaps because of their changing applicability to current events, exempla are a common characteristic — though not a necessary one — of many political advice texts throughout the Middle Ages. The stories might be inserted in an otherwise theoretical or practical discussion, as in Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes, or they might be found in a large collection of successive stories to show the vagaries of fortune, as in John Lydgate’s Fall of Princes. To modern audiences, like the (pseudo-)Aristotelian maxims, such collections of traditional stories often appear repetitive and unoriginal. However, several scholars have significantly nuanced the idea that exempla retained a monolithic meaning throughout the ages and have drawn attention to the contemporary relevance of de casibus narratives in their historical context.86

These three traditions — political theory and practical advice, collected wisdom from ancient sources, and de casibus — constituted the building blocks of all late medieval mirrors for princes, even if the precise content and scope could vary greatly. Or, as Matthew Giancarlo summarizes, “[n]ot all of the same elements are present to the same degree in every work, but they nonetheless make themselves felt across this textual field with something like the force of a genre, such that we can neither neatly divide the groupings by clear types or traits, nor house them comfortably under a single historical category.”87 The difficulty of defining this genre is particularly evident in the corpus of Middle English mirrors for princes. In addition to copies and translations of classical, Arabic, or contemporary Continental works, some original mirrors for princes were produced in medieval England. Among them are full-length works of political advice such as William of Pagula’s Speculum Regis Edwardi III and Thomas Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes, which, though drawing inspiration from earlier sources, address specific issues relevant to their English dedicatees.

Interestingly, however, Ashby credits none of these predecessors discussed so far — except the Liber Philosophorum — as the sources of inspiration for his own political tract. Ashby opens his poem with an acknowledgement of three other poetic forebears: Geoffrey Chaucer, John Lydgate, and John Gower. In doing so, Ashby places himself explicitly in the tradition of vernacular poetry rather than that of political tracts and mirrors for princes.88 Though neither Chaucer, Lydgate, nor Gower ever wrote a mirror for princes explicitly addressed to a ruler, unlike Hoccleve’s Regiment or Ashby’s Active Policy and Dicta, all three did engage with politics in their poetry in various ways. Indeed, many of the Ricardian and Lancastrian political texts that are nowadays usually counted amongst “mirrors for princes” are not independent political works, but sections on political advice embedded in larger fictional narratives, such as Chaucer’s Tale of Melibee from the Canterbury Tales, Book 7 of Gower’s Confessio Amantis, and large sections of Lydgate’s The Fall of Princes.89
Sources for The Active Policy and Dicta

Ashby probably knew and drew inspiration from texts of all three of these authors. The works of Lydgate he must surely have been familiar to him, since Ashby worked in Gloucester’s household at the time when the duke actively patronized Lydgate’s poetry. Yet Ashby leaves perhaps his most important influence unnoted: Hoccleve’s Regiment of Princes, the mirror written for Edward of Lancaster’s grandfather, Henry V. It is possible that Hoccleve and Ashby, both civil servants writing for a Lancastrian prince, were acquainted through their shared professional status, and it is probable that Ashby encountered Hoccleve’s poetical works. Robert Meyer-Lee, in his analysis of laureateship in Ashby’s poetry, sees “verbal echoes” and “the same stance” in both poets’ addresses to their princes, with both “expand[ing] the conventional epistolary opening to the high born into a mini-panegyric.”90 While Ashby explicitly acknowledges the direct influence of these poetic predecessors (except Hoccleve), the form of his work resembles more closely the traditional speculum of direct advice to a (future) ruler without a fictional framework, like Giles of Rome’s De regimine principum and John Fortescue’s De laudibus legum Angliae (In Praise of the Laws of England).

While the Active Policy is largely an original mirror for princes, like Hoccleve’s, the Dicta presents its advice in the form of translations in rhyme royal of Latin wisdom literature. In the preface of the Active Policy and Dicta, Ashby explicitly presents his text as a series of translations of such sententiae and not as an original mirror for princes.91 While the opening stanza quoted above places the work in the Middle English vernacular poetry tradition, the framing preface reveals the Latin sapiential tradition to be an equally important literary context for the work. Underlining his indebtedness to his Latin sources, Ashby precedes each of his translations in the Dicta with the original Latin passage. Unlike Ashby’s macaronic text, many vernacular translations of wise sayings only offer the translated text. A notable example is the Summum Sapientiae (also: Liber Proverbium or Sayings of Old Philosophers; DIMEV 5502),92 which was likely presented to Margaret of Anjou and may thus have been known to Ashby.93 Though fewer in number, there are other macaronic wisdom poems like Ashby’s Dicta, for instance the “Proverbs of Prophets, Poets, and Saints” (DIMEV 5529) which includes not only Latin and Middle English but also French.94 Perhaps the most famous didactic collection of sententiae that includes the Latin original alongside the vernacular translation is the Distichs of Cato, an originally third-century compilation of wise sayings that was a popular educational tool in medieval schools.

While Ashby was probably familiar with some of these texts, virtually all of his Latin quotations are taken from the previously mentioned collection known as the Liber Philosophorum. The Latin text which Ashby uses for his poem was based upon the originally Arabic text titled Mokhtâr el-Hikam, written in the eleventh century by the poet Abu’l Wefa Mubeschschir ben Fatik, probably an Egyptian emir from Damascus.95 Ancient philosophy was highly popular in the Muslim world, and the author of the Mokhtâr el-Hikam might have had access to a large array of Arabic translations of philosophers including Plato, Aristotle, and others. It is not precisely known on which texts he based his compilation, but his collection fits well into this burgeoning tradition of advice texts based on Greek philosophy which included the more popular Secretum Secretorum.96

The Mokhtâr el-Hikam found its way to the Christian world through Iberia: it was translated into Castilian in the first half of the thirteenth century as Bocados de Oro (Bits of Gold), to be followed by a Latin translation of this Spanish work in the latter half of the same century. The great popularity of this Liber Philosophorum is evidenced by the large number of surviving manuscripts.97 In the next century, this Latin version was eventually translated into French as the Dits Moraulx (Moral Sayings), which became very popular in fifteenth-century England.98 On the basis of this French version — which was still remarkably similar to the original Arabic text in terms of content and order — multiple English translations appeared in the fifteenth century, all now known under the title The Dicts and Sayings of the Philosophers: one by Stephen Scrope and another by an unknown translator both from around 1450, a reworking of Scrope’s version by William of Worcester from 1472, and finally a version by Anthony Woodville, Earl Rivers, which would rise to fame as one of the first texts printed in England by William Caxton in 1477.99 The latter in particular is interesting in light of the current subject: whereas Ashby used the Dicta to advise Prince Edward of Lancaster, the version of Woodville — who was the brother of Elizabeth Woodville, Edward IV’s queen — was written for the York heir, a young prince coincidentally also called Edward.100

The fact that two writers chose to use the Liber Philosophorum as the basis for their advice poem to a future prince in a time of such political upheaval shows that the text was seen to be especially relevant for the current circumstances, yet little has been said in scholarship about the content of the work in any of its incarnations. The length and density of the work may partly account for this scarcity of criticism. The Liber Philosophorum consists of a long enumeration of divergent pieces of advice on a vast range of topics, and it seems to lack a coherent message. The only apparent structure of the work is the division into chapters that each treat the views of one philosopher, such as Aristotle or Socrates, often preceded by a short biographical introduction. Otherwise, it is a rather haphazard collection of divergent admonitions, more reminiscent of an encyclopedia of wisdom than a narrative intended to be read from beginning to end. John William Sutton, in the introduction to his edition of the anonymous translation of the Dicts and Sayings, discerns one coherent theme, an “overall organizing principle,” in the collection: he believes the text to be “organized around the idea of oppositional logic.”101 The advice often juxtaposes contrasting concepts: good and bad, wisdom and folly, and so forth. In continually reinforcing the binary nature of morality, Sutton concludes, the text “follows many other sentential works in encouraging the kind of binary judgment that discourages free thinking and the questioning of authority.”102

Ashby’s Dicta is a unique text in the English Dicts tradition: it is the only Middle English translation to be directly based upon the Latin Liber Philosophorum rather than its French translation Dits Moraulx, and it is the only one to be written in verse. Moreover, it is not an attempt at a full translation like the other Middle English versions. Ashby abandons the structure of the original text, with its division into sections on individual philosophers. Instead, he inserts passages of varying length seemingly at random into his poem, jumping from one philosopher to another. (Perhaps this partly accounts for the fact that Ashby sometimes misattributes quotations.) In addition to the Latin preface written by Ashby himself (¶1), there are 189 Latin passages (¶¶2–190) which Ashby all attributes to a philosopher except one (for ¶5 he gives no source). Of these 188 passages which refer to a philosopher, 31 refer to the wrong one and 3 are partly misattributed.103 Curt Bühler notes that Ashby sometimes adds short phrases to the Latin sayings that might indicate influence from proverbial collections such as the Proverbiorum Liber (Book of Proverbs), or the Bible.104 Such divergences may of course be caused by differences in Ashby’s exemplar from the main manuscript tradition of the Liber Philosophorum used in modern editions. Since his exemplar has not been identified, it is at the moment impossible to judge the extent of Ashby’s own changes to his Latin source material, if any.105 What is possible, however, is a comparison between the Latin as Ashby incorporates it in his poem and his Middle English translations of it. His translation choices are highly revealing of Ashby’s main political concerns and convictions.

Apart from the Liber Philosophorum, Ashby made use of a couple of other sources. While virtually all Middle English stanzas without a Latin quotation are original verse composed by Ashby, critics have pointed out a few direct borrowings from other vernacular poems.106 An entire stanza (lines 688–94) is directly taken from Court of Sapience, a fifteenth-century wisdom poem:

lg.l: Woo worth debate that never may have pees!
Woo worth penaunce that asketh no pyte!
Woo worth vengeaunce that mercy may not cees!
Wo worth jugement that hath none equyte!
Wo worth that trouth that hath no charyte!
Woo worth that juge that may no gilty save!
And wo worth ryght that may no favour have!107

div.p: The Court of Sapience was written around the middle of the fifteenth century by an unknown author. Bühler suggests it might have been written by George Ashby, but both the Court’s editor Elizabeth Ruth Harvey and Margaret Kekewich reject this possibility, pointing to the many stylistic and thematic differences between the Court and Ashby’s known surviving work.108 In all probability Ashby borrowed the stanza from the Court rather than the other way around, as the original lines seem more at place within the context of the contemplative Court than in the Active Policy.109 If this is indeed the case, Ashby must have either committed the stanza to memory or have had access to a copy of the poem while he was composing the Active Policy.

Another direct borrowing, pointed out by Kekewich, is from a short anonymous poem on princely virtues known as “Seven Wise Counsels” (DIMEV 939).110 Each of the seven stanzas concerns a different princely virtue; the stanza entitled “temperancia” reads as follows:

lg.l: Thynge past remember and wele devide
Thynge present considere & wele govenegovern
Ffor thynge commynge prudently provide
Peise matiers or thou dome or disterneWeigh; before; judge or make decisions
Lat ryght in cause holde the lanternLet righteousness be the guide in matters (of judgment)
Bytwene frendys & foon stonde even & egallimpartial and equal
And for no mede be not parciall.111gift (reward)

div.p: The first three lines of this stanza are adopted almost word-for-word by Ashby in stanza 131, the final stanza of the first half of the text, the Active Policy:

lg.l: Thinges past, remembre and wele devide;
Thinges present, considre and wele governe;
For thinges commyng, prudently provide.

div.p: On the basis of the manuscript context of “Seven Wise Counsels,” Kekewich believes the poem to have been written most likely in the early 1450s, which means that Ashby must have borrowed the lines from this poem rather than the other way around.
The manuscript

The Active Policy and Dicta survives in a single manuscript: Cambridge University Library, MS Mm.4.42. In its current form, the manuscript consists of six full vellum quires of eight leaves, which measure around 270 x 180 mm, though the leaves are not all of equal size. The size of the written space is 190 x 100 mm. The current quarter-bound binding, combining morocco leather for the spine with marbled paper on the pasteboards, dates from the twentieth century. A note on the inside of the front cover identifies the binder as Douglas Cockerell & Son, Grantchester, made in December 1968.

The manuscript as it survives is incomplete: the poem ends in the middle of the 312th stanza. Since the last quire of the manuscript is complete, this suggests that at least an entire quire is missing, though it remains impossible to tell how much of the text is lost. There is no indication in the Dicta that Ashby was working towards a conclusion, nor did he make a systematic translation of his source text on the basis of which it would be possible determine whether it was nearly finished. It is even unclear if Ashby ever completed the main text. The manuscript seems unfinished: room has been left for the insertion of capitals, which are now only visible as small penciled minuscules. These appear on fols. 2r, 2v, 4r, 5r, 6v, 9v, and 19r, each time marking the start of a new passage, usually preceded by a Latin heading: the prose preface (fol. 2r), the start of the Middle English verse (fol. 2v), the start of The Active Policy of a Prince (fol. 4r), the sections discussing the past (fol. 5r), the present (fol. 6v), and the future (fol. 9v), and finally the start of the Dicta et Opiniones Diversorum Philosophorum (fol. 19r).

The whole text is presented in single columns, averaging 28 lines or four 7-line stanzas per page in a Signet Secretary script.112 The first page, containing a Latin prose preface identifying George Ashby as the author of the text, is badly damaged, rendering the text at points illegible. The final folio of the manuscript in its current form, fol. 48v, is also slightly worn, suggesting that it may have served as the back cover before being bound in its current twentieth-century binding. The manuscript contains no decoration, and there are few indications of later owners or use.

CUL MS Mm.4.42 is humble in appearance. The unremarkable look of the manuscript has led some critics to believe that this could not have been the original copy meant as a presentation piece for Prince Edward,113 while others assume the current text to be corrupted by the emendations of a later scribe.114 However, Sobecki’s recent identification of CUL MS Mm.4.42 as a holograph means that, exceptionally for a medieval text, we have a single authoritative reading of the Active Policy and Dicta.115

It is unknown whether the manuscript ever reached its intended recipient, Prince Edward of Lancaster.
