The unfinished state might suggest that it did not, though that is not conclusive evidence.116 The earliest evidence of later ownership is in the collection of John Moore, Bishop of Ely.117 An avid book collector, Moore’s acquisitions resulted in what has been called “the most important private library” of its time, the contents of which ranged from “rough notes and commonplace books of little or no value” to “priceless medieval volumes of acknowledged importance.”118 The divergent nature of books included in his collection makes it difficult to assign a particular reason for the presence of Ashby’s mirror among them — it seems most likely that the manuscript joined the collection by chance, as part of a private library acquired by Moore. Upon the bishop’s death in 1714, his vast collection of medieval and early printed books was bought by King George I and donated to Cambridge University Library, forming the Royal collection. An eighteenth-century engraving bearing George I’s arms is still pasted on the inside of the twentieth-century binding. Unfortunately, the drastic rebinding of Moore’s volumes when they joined the Royal library in Cambridge resulted in the loss of many earlier user and owner traces, because the original flyleaves and bindings were destroyed. For many of the manuscripts once belonging to John Moore’s collection, including CUL MS Mm.4.42, then, there is no evidence of their provenance before they entered the bishop’s library.119
Editorial principles

The following critical edition and translation of the Active Policy and Dicta is based on the only surviving copy of the work, preserved in CUL MS Mm.4.42. The Active Policy and Dicta is a macaronic text, combining Middle English verse and Latin prose. In accordance with METS style, the verse and prose passages are numbered separately. The edition therefore switches between line numbers for Middle English verse and paragraph numbers for Latin prose, and both the textual and explanatory notes are keyed accordingly. New paragraph numbers are assigned to quotes citing a different philosopher, even if it directly follows another Latin quote (see ¶¶31–33). Modern English translations of the Latin passages are provided in the footnotes.

Since CUL MS Mm.4.42 is a holograph, it represents the text as Ashby wrote it. In many respects, working from a single manuscript written by the author makes the work of the modern editor significantly easier: the surviving copy is an authoritative one, not corrupted by mistakes or conscious changes by later scribes. On the other hand, the author-scribe, too, is liable to making mistakes. While I have stayed as close as possible to the original text, the goal of providing an accessible edition of the work means that I have made a number of changes and emendations to the text as written by Ashby.

Some of these are systematic changes to make the text correspond to modern spelling conventions. I have retained most of the original orthography of the text, but made a few exceptions: in both the Middle English verse and the Latin prose, I have given the modern orthography for u/v (have for haue, ubi for vbi), and only in the Middle English for i/j and þ (th). This means that I have edited iust to just and obieccion to objeccion in Middle English, but retained the initial i in the Latin (iusticiam). I have standardized irregular spelling variations of other writer’s names. For instance, Ashby once writes Pitogoras for Pitagoras and Socratas for Socrates, which I have silently emended to one standard spelling; similarly, I have standardized Chauucer (line 1) to Chaucer. At some points, the damage to the manuscript renders parts of the text illegible. I have indicated those passages with ellipses. The Textual Notes provide plausible readings where possible.

All abbreviations, in both the Middle English and the Latin, have been expanded. These include the ampersands (and or et) which Ashby uses irregularly in both languages. On the whole, Ashby’s abbreviations of letters are regular; the one exception is a curved dash in the Middle English sections, appearing inconsistently, often above the final word of a line. While it may appear at first to indicate an abbreviation of ou, the absence of the curved dash in other cases suggests it does not represent omitted letters, as that would occasionally create problems with the rhyme scheme, while on other folios the dash does not appear at all. Where this dash appears above other syllables in the Middle English text, I have similarly interpreted it as a form of decoration rather than an abbreviation, due to its irregular occurrence. The curved dash also appears in the Latin sections, but here it is used as a general indicator of an abbreviation. While Ashby uses some fixed abbreviations for a specific set of letters (the common abbreviations of per, pro, ter, quia, for instance), in many cases he simply indicates that a word is abbreviated by adding the curved dash above it, indicating, for example, that pctori should be read as peccatori and dra as differencia. All such abbreviations have been silently expanded, where needed on the basis of the Liber.

Capitalization and punctuation are modern. Similarly, I have standardized word separation in both the Middle English and the Latin, either by dividing one word into two or combining two words into one. For instance, the Middle English a bove is given as above and shalbe as shal be, while the Latin econtra is emended to e contra. While Ashby is not consistent in his word separation, I have consistently made such changes to reflect modern spelling conventions. Two further systematic changes to the Middle English are meant to facilitate ease of reading for the modern reader. Firstly, Ashby often elides to or the with the following word if it starts with a vowel: for instance, topteine and thextent. In such cases, I have added an apostrophe to signal that these should be read as two separate, but combined words: t’opteine and th’extent. Secondly, Ashby forms the possessive most often by adding a separate is to a noun: the possessive of man is thus written as man is, and of people as people is. Because this looks like a verb rather than a form of the genitive to the modern reader, I have merged these into one word (manis, peopleis), providing glosses where necessary. These silent emendations aimed at standardizing the text (capitalization, word separation, elisions, and expansions of abbreviations) are not included in the Textual Notes.

In addition to these consistent changes in capitalization, punctuation, and spelling, I have corrected all the obvious errors in the Middle English as well as grammatical errors whenever necessary to ease reading comprehension. The former category includes missing or wrong letters (perfourmyg is emended to perfourmyng, and childred to children). The latter category is less clear-cut: it mostly concerns missing words, without which the grammatical structure of the sentence becomes difficult to grasp. For instance, line 1582 originally read “Thanke God that ye nat therof culpable,” which I have emended to “Thanke God that ye be nat therof culpable,” while I have changed line 1629 from “How shuld put in suche oon affiance” to “How shuld ye put in suche oon affiance.” For all of these irregular emendations, I have noted the original reading in a Textual Note.

The emendations of the Latin passages pose a particular challenge. In general, I have retained the original spelling of the Latin, in line with common characteristics of medieval Latin. That means c might be used for t (pocius or potius), and e for ae (querit for quaerit). As in the Middle English, obvious spelling mistakes have been corrected (e.g., familialitas to familiaritas). Less straightforward are the apparent grammatical or semantic mistakes in Ashby’s Latin passages. Almost all of Ashby’s quotations are from the Liber, of which hundreds of copies were made in the medieval West. The edition by Ezio Franceschini is based on one of the manuscript branches, though he gives many significant variations in the footnotes. Most of the differences between Ashby’s passages and Franceschini’s edition are only minor, but in some instances the Latin given by Ashby varies significantly from the published edition of the Liber Philosophorum. While many of these differences simply change the nuance or the order of the philosopher’s lessons, some of them result in grammar mistakes or significant changes in meaning. In general, I always favor Ashby’s rendition of the sayings over those in the edition of the Liber Philosophorum, except in those cases where Ashby’s quotation becomes untranslatable because words are missing or appear in the wrong case. I will give a few examples:
div.quote: Dicta: Si rex omittit investigare populi sui facta, milicie sue, et inimicorum, non uno die securus de regno suo. Hec Hermes.
Liber Philosophorum: Si rex omitat investigare populi sui facta, milicie sue et inimicorum, non erit uno die securus de regno suo.120
div.p: There are two differences between these renditions: the conjugation of the first finite verb omittere (indicative in Dicta, subjunctive in Liber Philosophorum) and the presence of the second finite verb erit, which is missing from the Dicta. Whereas the former difference does not significantly impact the meaning of either statement and can thus be left as such, the omission of erit in Ashby’s version means that this passage cannot be translated without adding a verb. I have therefore emended his quotation with the help of the Liber variant to the following:
div.quote: Emended Dicta: Si rex omittit investigare populi sui facta, milicie sue, et inimicorum, non erit uno die securus de regno suo. Hec Hermes. (¶70)
Translation: If a king neglects to investigate the deeds of his people, his army, and his enemies, not one day will he be secure in his reign. Thus Hermes.
div.p: In another instance, I have made both an emendation to Ashby’s Latin on the basis of the Liber Philosophorum, and have used the Liber variant to help me translate Ashby’s quotation:
div.quote: Dicta: Bonum est loqui dicere modicum, racione completum, est respondere laudabiliter et confestim. Hec Aristotiles.
Liber Philosophorum: Cui dixit quidam: quid est bene loqui? Respondit: dicere modicum ratione completum et respondere laudabiliter et confestim.121
div.p: The Dicta’s second est renders the grammar of the Latin impossible to translate, and it seems to be a copying mistake of et, as it is given in the Liber Philosophorum. I have therefore emended it accordingly. The differences at the start of the passage are more significant. While I retain Ashby’s version of the Latin passage, the double infinitive verbs loqui and dicere — synonyms for “to speak” — seem to be the result of a combination of the question and answer in the Liber Philosophorum’s version. I have signaled this mistake in a textual note and have omitted one of the synonyms in my translation.
div.quote: Emended Dicta: Bonum est loqui dicere modicum, racione completum, et respondere laudabiliter et confestim. Hec Aristotiles. (¶146)
Translation: It is good to speak little, complete with reason, and to respond laudably and immediately. Thus Aristotle.
div.p: My translations are all based on Ashby’s Latin rather than on the Liber Philosophorum, though as this example shows in some cases the latter served as a useful tool for elucidating the sense or structure of Ashby’s quotation. In general, I have stayed as close as possible to the meaning and grammar of the Latin. In order to avoid awkward English translations, a completely faithful translation is not always preferable, especially of complex verb forms or successions of noun phrases. I have therefore attempted to strike a balance between translations that are comprehensible while at the same time accurately reflecting the meaning of the Latin passage, so that the reader may compare them to Ashby’s often rather loose translations into Middle English.

The goal of this edition is to present Ashby’s text as accurately as possible, while making it accessible to the modern reader by emending the spelling where necessary and providing additional textual and explanatory comments in the notes. As such, the few traces of later readers are not included in the edition. These traces, consisting of some penciled lines under parts of the text and hashtag-symbols in the margin, are not contemporary with the composition of the poem, nor do they contain text that engages with the poem. For these reasons, these traces do not form a part of the present edition. The manuscript contains no illustrations, decoration, marginalia, or illuminated capitals that are contemporary with the text. Room has been left for the insertion of initials, which were never added, and now only appear as small penciled letters. These are included in the Textual Notes.
